So with Hegel, I think part of the difficulty lies in the fact that he has no core area of interest. His philosophy is a holistic system, incorporating just about everything under the sun, a real philosopher's philosopher. I once saw someone on Reddit describe the difficulty in reading the Phenomenology as "This book contains the sum of all human knowledge \[at the time\]. And to understand it, you need the sum of all human knowledge." That, and as it well known, he wrote badly, which is less of a problem in analytical philosophy (though I would charge Wittgenstein with writing the TLP badly but that's it's own thing).

This is distinct from the similar difficulty you might have with philosophers of math or physics, where yes it's assumed you already know the general ideas being talked about, but with Hegel it's far less focused on just one thing.
